verdict.root_cause: At 20:14:34 UTC an automated platform process (platform-automation) lowered the container memory limit on frauddetection-service to 200m. Within about twelve seconds the service entered a sustained crash/restart loop: normal Kafka consumption logging stops at ~20:11:34 and from ~20:14:46 the log stream is nothing but repeated JVM/container startup sequences on a near-constant ~62s cadence through 20:21:47, with no application exception, stack trace, or ERROR line anywhere. That signature — JVM boots successfully through JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS pickup and the OpenTelemetry agent banner, then dies silently before doing any work, over and over — is the signature of the kernel killing the process for exceeding its memory ceiling rather than of an application fault, a bad artifact, or a slow dependency. Nothing else changed on the service in the window: no deploy, no image change, no flag flip. The failing mechanism is the process being unable to fit in the memory it is allowed to occupy and being terminated for it; the automated limit edit is how that state was entered, not the mechanism itself.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent strands converge. (1) tr_31d1c0de5ce5 establishes a single change on the service in the window — a memory-limit reduction to 200m at 20:14:34 by an automated actor — and explicitly rules out deploy, image rollout, flag flip, and change-quiescence, which removes bad_deploy from contention on the change side. (2) tr_2c73ddd81f41 dates the onset of the crash loop to ~20:14:46, twelve seconds after the limit edit, and characterizes it as at least eight startup cycles on a ~62s cadence rather than a one-off restart; it further rules out the process failing before JVM init (the agent banner is reached each cycle) and rules out any logged application error, downstream timeout, or deserialization fault. A process that reaches instrumentation initialization and then vanishes without emitting a single error line is being terminated externally, not throwing. That excludes dependency_latency as the mechanism — a slow dependency produces timeouts and waiting requests, not silent process death, and there is no such evidence. (3) The absence of the process explains the metric gaps: tr_afd8a69b1f68 and tr_5ab891e1f922 both return no series at all for calls_total, numerator and denominator alike, which is consistent with a service that is not staying alive long enough to emit spans, though both results correctly note that an empty match is absence of series and not a measured zero. Classification: the guidance is that a limit lowered until a process is killed for exceeding it is resource_exhaustion — the edit is how it started, exhaustion is what is happening. The service is failing now because it cannot fit in its memory ceiling, so restoring the prior limit (config_revert) is the fix that resolves it; a restart alone would only re-enter the loop. Confidence is held at medium rather than high because the OOM mechanism is inferred from timing and log shape and was never directly confirmed: tr_5ab891e1f922 explicitly rules out that any metric evidence supports the working-set/OOMKill chain, because no container memory, limit, or last_terminated_reason series were ever queried.
open_questions: No direct confirmation of OOMKill: kube_pod_container_resource_limits, container_memory_working_set_bytes, and pod last_terminated_reason / exit code 137 were never queried (tr_5ab891e1f922 states the hypothesis is entirely unverified, not supported). The mechanism is inferred from timing plus silent-death log shape.
The prior memory limit is not recorded (tr_31d1c0de5ce5), so the magnitude of the reduction and whether the JVM heap configuration was ever compatible with 200m cannot be determined.

The literal value '200m' is a milli-unit suffix, which for a memory quantity would be a fractional byte rather than 200 MiB. If the automation emitted a CPU-style unit into a memory field, the value is malformed rather than merely small — that would shift the reading toward bad_config. Nothing in the dispatches resolves whether '200m' is the raw spec value or a rendering artifact of the change log.

Whether calls_total is absent because the service is dead or because frauddetectionservice was never instrumented under that service_name label is unresolved (tr_afd8a69b1f68, tr_5ab891e1f922); an empty result cannot distinguish these, so the crash loop's traffic impact is unquantified.

The log stream stops entirely at 20:21:47, ~3.5 minutes before window end (tr_2c73ddd81f41, low confidence). Whether the pod entered CrashLoopBackOff, was descheduled, or logging simply failed is unknown — as is the current state of the service at the time of this verdict.
Blast radius beyond frauddetectionservice was not investigated. Kafka consumption halted at ~20:11:34; the effect on order/fraud-check backlog and on upstream producers is unmeasured.
What triggered platform-automation to rightsize this container, and whether the same automation has applied or will apply similar limits to other services, is unexamined — this bears on recurrence.
